blocks.x: I just want to get down where we're doing this. We're doing it at your home at 700 Thales Street. That's in Algiers. And what's your name? Charles E. Love. And my name is Dick Allen. And you got a name? Marjorie Zander. All right. We won't leave you out. I'm always scared I'm going to leave me out. You know I forget that half the time. To leave my name and I want the secretary to know what it's all about when she hears it. You were going to sing a song for us?
Well I can sing the chorus of that hoodoo song. I'll sing the chorus of it. I don't know
how many voices. Okay. Well just give it a shot you know. Go ahead.

I've been hoodooed. I've been hoodooed. I've been hoodooed by a big black coon. I've been hoodooed. I've been hoodooed. I've been hoodooed by a boyly coon. He got a rabbit foot and bunnied with a frog. He placed it in the end of an old hollow log. Right on the road wide to pass along. Ever since then I've been feeling wrong. I've been hoodooed. I've been hoodooed. I've been hoodooed by a big black coon. I've been hoodooed. I've been hoodooed by a boyly coon. That's about all I know of that. I used to sing a long while ago and play guitar you know with the music. But I forgot the words of it you know. I used to make up little verses like that. And after you sing one verse then you sing another coon. One verse then another coon. About how old were you then? Oh I was a kid. I was 16 or 17 years old.
I see. And you were born in 1880 uh what 1880 something huh?
1885. November the s- October the 6th.
So that's been around the turn of the century around that?
1985 yeah.
You don't have today's date on that.
Yeah that's right I don't. What is today's date?
Today's date. Today is uh? Sunday was Mother's Day.
Yeah it's May the uh.
Sunday was the 8th.
Yeah so it makes it May the 10th of 1960. Uh. Let's see.

Now what what about hoodoo in those days? Did people believe in it much? Oh yeah there's a lot of people believe in that up until now. Well is that right? Yeah but they used to believe in it and then they used to have songs about it. That's one of the old hoodoo songs.
They had many songs about it?
Oh yeah. They had Marie LaVoe. They had a song about her you know. Marie LaVoe.
Which song is that? Is that the one Sellefman?
That's the one Sellefman used to play. He used to sing it.
How long ago did he sing that?
Well he sang it all along. Oh. While he played you know.
Well he's been singing that song for years.
Oh for years yeah. Whenever you asked him like that he'd sing it.
Any other songs about hoodoo?

But this this song when I was telling you about this now I've been hoodoo. They used to sing that in all them old ministry shows long while ago. 1903. Billy Cassand used to sing that in his ministry. You remember you heard of Billy Cassand? Oh sure. Of course he's a famous man. I went I was waiting for a little show they called Overton and Senior Ragtime Minister Show. And he was he just had got by and he went on a honeymoon trip. He just went out with the show. Opened up the show. And he he thought about Bill Cassand you know. His son got Bill Cassand and his wife because they had never went in the state of Mississippi. And he got about $400 a week. We had a ragtime ministry show, you know. And he used to use that number then. That was about 1903. I've been hoodooed. At the end of his song, he would start to pull off his vests, you know. He was a great big fan. He had about, looked like about 50 of them vests on, loud vests, you know. And the last one would be a corset. A lady's corset. And he'd on fast and that, you know. And then he'd grab his suspenders and his wife would catch him, you know. Catch him and bring him off the stage, you know. The old fella tore his last. I made the last trip with him in Mississippi. Let me see what year that was. I can't think of the exact year. Trying to think, no.
Would it be before depression?
Huh?
Would it be before depression?
Oh, yeah. Way before that. Nineteen. Around 1916 or something like that.
Just before we got in the war then, huh?
Yeah.
Around that time.

Billy Cassand had never been in Mississippi, you see. So they used his name on the car and he'd done that act on the stage, him and his wife. And he was forgetful, you know. His wife was named Louisa. She was a fine person. She was highly educated, you know. She learned him what he knew. He used to be a little shoeshine boy in Donisonville. And he had a big, funny looking mouth, you know. And he was really funny. He was apt and catching that foolishness. And she'd teach it to him. And towards last, they both was old. She was a good singer. And he used to forget his line, you know. But he had a word he used to say when he forget, you know. And she'd catch on to it. She'd know that word, you know. And you hear him say, Oh, Father, take my hand. I got full king. You know, that's telling her that he done forgot his line. And she'd just look around like that. The audience wouldn't notice it. And she'd just wake her mouth. And he could read her lips, you know. And he'd catch on, you know. He'd say, I know he's. He'd be kidding all the time. I know he's. I don't know what I'd do if it wasn't for you, you know. We could go and we was down in the pit, you know. That was a funny fellow.
You remember any of his jokes or anything?

Huh? Well, I don't forgot all them old jokes. They was old funny jokes anyhow, you know. He tells a guy that he known. He'd be telling the chicken about, telling the people that he didn't like chicken very much, you know. And all that kind of stuff. He said, but he'd have one on the Sunday if he had to buy one. He must have been stealing them all the time. Yeah. He said, I don't have a chicken all the Sunday if I had to steal one. If I had to buy one. He said, but I don't like chicken very much. He said, I don't like nothing about a chicken but his neck. But his head. And his neck. And the two wings. Out there, I'd say, and the back. You know, and the people would laugh. He'd let them laugh. Well, I think he was finished, you know. He'd say, and the toes. And the egg back. Oh, he'd go on down until there wasn't no more chicken. Then the people would laugh again, you know. I think he was finished. In time, you say that, and he'd stop that, you know. He'd say, I would have eat the feathers, but they're too hard to clean. He went over in England. He couldn't, there was a queen over there. Nobody couldn't make her laugh. Belka Sandshue was over there and went before the queen, you know. And they say that if he'd make her laugh, that she'd give him a fine present, you know. She was a solemn person. Oh, he'd done all his tricks. She'd pull all them vests off, you know. Louisa grabbed him and brought him on out. That wouldn't make her laugh. So they was having tea, you know. They drinks tea over in England, regular. And they had those little cups, you know. They're small. But they're too big for a person to sit in their mouth, you know. They were sitting to the table, and he done tried to make her laugh all kinds of ways. She wouldn't laugh. So they start to drink the tea, you know. He just took the cup and sauce and put it all in his mouth. They had to get a towel. She had a hysteric, man. She laughed. She give him a diamond about big as your finger there. That big diamond, gold handle, umbrella. Walk the stick with a gold knob on it. He brought that back. He gave him a lot of money, too. He sure went busted around. Let me see. Just before I got on that Overton Senior show, she told us on the show, she used to talk with we boys in the daytime. She said, Billy would spend about two, three fortunes. He would go up to the Elks' places like that, you know, all up when he'd get around New York, them big places. And he'd spend too much money and he'd drink so much until he'd be sick, you know, all the time. His wife was worried. They had a state loan on the course. She used to go out at night and pay high as $10, $15 cab fare, you know, going around looking for him. To bring him in, you see. He'd be in the Elks' place somewhere and drink a lot of champagne. He'd want to be a big shot like the rest of the fellas, you know. He'd buy too much champagne and he'd be sick all the next day. So she'd go look for him. A poor Billy would come on in. Well, we had a fella on the show called John Johnston. He was a great big fella, about six foot four. And he wore suits with big stripes, you know, a great big stripe. He used to wear fine clothes, you know. And he was so big and he looked so much different from the other fellas in Mississippi. Every time we'd go to, you know, they'd say, oh, that's Billy Cassand there, you know. And he just had to be Billy Cassand. They'd say, what's your name? He'd say, that's all right, but it's Billy. And he'd carry him on downtown the gang of fellas, you know. And give him champagne, fill his pocket up with cigar. He'd come back late at night, you know. And he'd say, you're Louisa. That's the way he'd call me, you know. What you say, Billy? Well, Louisa wouldn't let him out when we went over there in Mississippi. John Johnston, they'd take him all the time down to the Elks. He'd come back with cigars and everything. And Billy Cassand knows what he was doing, you know. Got on to what he was doing. He'd say, Louisa, I don't like that fella there. He was misrepresenting. He says, I don't like him. And we had a trombone player called Floyd Mike Miller. He used to play with the cattle band in Shreepo. He used to do it for them, man. He used to stand alongside the cars, you know. And Miss Cassand would come off. He'd get in a conversation with him, you know. And after a while, year come John, he'd light out and go downtown somewhere and get her plenty to drink, you know. Highballs and stuff like that. They think it'd be Billy Cassand. He'd come back laughing and John would laugh at him, you know. Man, this world, old man, the death. Louisa, I don't like that fella. In Florida, he'd be across the street killing himself laughing, getting his kicks, you know. Louisa.
Before I forget it, I don't think we put on the tape in that hoodoo song. You say, I've been hoodooed by a big black coon.
Coon, yeah.
And what does that mean?
That means big black man. Mm-hmm. Big black man.
Another thing I wanted to ask you is when did you come to New Orleans the first time here, remember?

The first time? Mm-hmm. Oh, I used to partly live down there when I was a kid, you know. My mother, she used to go out with my father like that. She used to sing sometimes. Mm-hmm. We'd have kind of a little show like with the man. And I was a baby. Well, my cousin, she lives up in Grittling now. She used to have me with her all the time, mine and me, you know, babysitter. So she take me from Platt when she lived down there on that canal back there. Take me down there. And I was a baby around there. When I went home, I missed her. I used to, you know how it is when a kid gets used to a nurse. I used to want to see her, you know. So mama brought me down there when I was wearing short pants. I must have been about five or six years old. And I stayed around there. And I'd miss mama and them go to crime. She'd send me back to Plattman, you know. Send me back home. Well, after I got to be a big boy, around 10, 11, and 12, up to about 16 years old, I stayed down there with my cousin, Henrietta. She was living right there on New Nez Street.
Well, we had a little discussion. When did they start putting the screen in on street cars? When you came down here at the first, could everybody sit together and mix it up?

Yes, when I was down there when I was a kid. But I think when they put the screen on, I was in Shreepo. I couldn't carry this around. Must have been around 1950 or somewhere along there. Because that rich fella that owned the radio system there in Shreepo, Mr. Sawyer or something like that. I don't know, I forgot his name. He lived on Texas Avenue. He come down here to help you fight that thing. But they lost. They put the screen on the car. And they put it on in Shreepo too.
Well then really, I was a youngster now. Segregation, that segregation business, has come in more since that time.
Oh yeah. Well, it was around 1950, I guess. Something like that.
It wasn't as bad in those days.
It wasn't so bad, no. Got bad on account of fellas got loud, you know. A lot of common people coming into the city. They're located on Franklin Street.
I know about that.

Franklin and North Ramport all around in there. Even on Dried Street. They were loud. People wouldn't live in the neighborhood with them, you know. They were always getting arrested, put in jail. That was a tough place up there, around Franklin.
Gasket Street?
Ever been on? Franklin and Padilla.
Ever been on Gasket Street?
Gasket, let's see.
That's around Cleveland? You know where Cleveland is? Two or three blocks above Canal, you know, between Tulane and Canal, that section.
Cleveland? Cleveland? That's out by the Straight University.
No. Uh. Well, I guess Straight University used to be back that way, I'm trying to remember.
But... 25 blocks back Canal Street. Yeah.
What I'm talking about is between Claiborne and Ramport, and between Tulane and Canal, in that area. You know right in there where I'm talking about?
Claiborne.
You know where Larry and Cat's liquor store is?
I know where you're talking about.
I don't mind Charity Hospital, so...
Well, between Charity and Canal.
Oh, yeah. Yeah, I'd be all around in there.
What was going on there?
That was a rough part of town, too.
Fast women?
Yeah, around Harvard. Fast everything. That was a tough part of the city.
Mm-hmm.
Called that the battlefield back in there. Mm-hmm. Back in Tulane. And Chinatown was right on... Common Street there, right across from Ramport. My first precinct. Was down on the next corner.
They used to have some wild things going on there, too, didn't they?

The other Chinatown used to kill one another and hide it. Yeah, they big odds say, you seen two Chinatown sitting down on the floor with a sharp hatchet, cutting one another up. Oh. The one would die, you know, they'd just open up the floor and bury them right there. They found a whole lot of bones around there, you know. That's too common. Common Street.
I didn't know they ever had a Chinatown here.
Yeah, they had a Chinatown, yeah. They had a Chinatown in Alexander. Used to sell dope. Well, I seen them sell some stuff like gunpowder. It looked like a little bit of box. They smoked that.
Well, what happened to it? What happened to all the Chinatowns?

They, I don't know, they'd run them out of here, depoiled them. They wouldn't tell them on one another, you know. Every now and then one come up missing, they didn't know where he was at. Nobody know nothing about him. And nobody stayed in that old building but Chinatowns from Ramport to Tulane. The building come out in a ship like that, in a D-ship.
Common? It's around Common and Ramport and Tulane in that neighborhood.
Yeah, right in there.
They would smoke opium and all that stuff, huh?

Oh, cottage stuff. You could go there, they had a place that slipped you in there and you could smoke, you know, while you're in there and come out, pay for it and everything, but Chinese don't know nothing. Never know anything what you're talking about. They call it Chinatown.
Did many of the musicians smoke that stuff?
Oh, they had a lot of fellas that used to do that. Smoke opium? Smoke hop.
Yeah, smoke hop.

That's what I'm talking about. Yeah, some kind of stuff to fix up. Moe's Chelsea in Shreeport. Man, the Patterson, we caught up with him, you know, we know he's smoking something. So we had a job down in Mansfield, you see. We all had to get room to sleep that night. So Moe's got him a room by himself, you know, and he had a whole suitcase with him besides his Violet case, you know. Man, he said, we gonna have some fun tonight when we get off from that dam. We got off from the dance, you know, and Moe went in his room, put on some pink pajamas, went in there and while he was out in the back somewhere that man he went and looked in the suitcase and man, he had a pipe in there that looked like a clarinet. You know, the one Piku played, go down and come back up and well, that's why he put that stuff in there, you know. He hold that over there and he's smoking. Had holes on there too, you know, let stuff come out. Man, he said, look here, I didn't know Moe was a clarinet player. He said, this guy got a fucking little instrument of clarinet. And he said, let's steal it and see what he's gonna do and see how he's gonna act. So we stole that clarinet where he had that hot pipe, brought it in and hit it. Moe was coming in, you know, and he went to get his smoke. He looked in his suitcase, that pipe was gone. Boy, you oughta heard the talk. He put on there. He said, anybody got my pipe? He said, they take that, they ain't no man. He said, I'd kill him if I know who took him. Nobody answered the word, you know, because two, three of them fellas stole that pipe, you see. they just went on and took what he said. Now he raised some sand. When he went out somewhere in town, they slipped it back in his grip, you know, and he come back. Now he raised sand again. He smoked that pipe so much till he come out, he was a black man, but he looked like a China.
Changed his color, huh?
Mm-hmm. He was real dark? He was a real dark fella, but he come after looking like a black China when he smoked so much.
He had slanty eyes and everything?
His eyes got that way. He kind of looked like a China when I know but he was a black fella. A violin player.
Did it change his color, really?
Mm-hmm.
Made him lighter?
Made him darker.
Oh, darker. Wait a minute, I'll turn it off.
Black China.
You say he had a pretty good band in three parts that far?
Yeah.
What was his name?
Moe Shelson.
Is he still alive, you think?
I don't know. Moe smoked so much of that stuff I guess he's about dead now. I never hear from him anymore.
I was going to ask you about the Red Book. Oh, yeah. How many bands played the Red Book that you know of?
Let's see. Superior Band down there. Pete played with them sometimes.
Pete Bococci.

Yeah. He played by Bronk Johnson playing the trumpet. And Harry Walker in Alexander. Well, they had some different bands around there. You know, they all played the Red Book. We was all connected together, you see. We had a big orchestra used to rehearse every Sunday. We just rehearsed over to them. And we'd invite all the musicians to that rehearsal, you know, a bunch of men. Every Sunday, there was Baby Lovey. he was a drummer. He was in Kansas City now, with Lee's band. And they had some bands around there, fake bands, you know, just fake music. They could play the same right, they hear them so much, you know. They'd play them just like the man that was reading. That was Bunk Johnson's uncle.
Bunk Johnson's uncle?

Yeah, Bunk, his uncle was named Willie Young. He was a violin player. He used to play violin, guitar and band. He was around Alexander at that time. Bunk wasn't that or Bunk was there. It was around 19, 8, 9, 10.
Was he strictly a faker, Willie Young?

Yeah, strictly a faker. He played them right just like the real musicians and he heard them so much, you know. We used to play them every night. We'd work in a district over that body there, you know. That was the district there. About 18 bands over there. Pensacola, Kid from Florida. He was a good violin player. And Zoo Robinson, trombone player. He used to know.
Who did he work with?
He worked with Baby Lovett and Mo Johnson, Pensacola Kid, and Willie Reed, bass player. Used to work for Miss, let me see,
what's it,
Lucille Agnes. I used to work for Pines and Blanches. I worked two, three different places, Pines and Blanches, Miss B. Nichols, Lucille Wilson.
These were all the madams, huh?

Huh? Yeah, he called them madams. House lady, you know, blind lady. I worked in Alexander, I believe it was 1970 or 8, they had high water. The Bay Rapids swore up, you see, we had to go over a bridge to go the way. And the water got so high they had to move from downstairs to upstairs on the front porch. We'd go to wake and skiff. Man, the water got up to the top, the first floor, you know. You just get right out to skiff and go right in the building. The water went in the building one night, about one inch. And I left and come back to Plagman, you know. I said, I ain't going back up there until that water go around. The water went down, they had to rebuild, fix up, I went back.
Well, when you were playing in different places all over the state, did they ever used to have brass bands for funerals in any place except here?

No, only in New Orleans. But, we built a musician in Alexander, they called him Ollie. Ollie Williams or something like that. He got killed by a train. And the musicians didn't have no union there, but they were all friends, they had a club like, you know. And this was a strange fella he comes out of shop somewhere. He didn't have no people and nothing so we just put in five and six dollars a piece, you know, give him a big funeral and got all the fellas in them different bands. We had about a 50 piece band to play for his funeral.
About when was that?

And I was the one that conducted the funeral. Just a few of them had seen a funeral down there, you know. I had to show them how to walk and line them up, you know. We didn't have no funeral markers, so we had one flea as a bird. And I played in the air, oh my God to thee, and a few hymns what I could remember I used to hear down there, you know. And coming back from the funeral we played all them rags, you know, coming back like we do here. That was in 1908. That was way back when.
That was around the time of the high water?
Huh?
That was around the time of that high

water? Yeah, right after the water went down. This boy got killed in the St. Louis Watkins Iron Mountain run out that way. He was talking to someone on the train and pulled up, you know, and he slipped and fell. Train run right over his neck crazy head off. What
did he play, this guy?
Baseball they play.
But they were playing the same things for funerals then that they play now?

No, it wasn't out of the money, you see. They didn't know nothing but the air, oh my God, that they in a few little hymns like that, you know. hymns out of any little book, play any kind of sacred music. It didn't have but that one thing that we buried in, the musicians, you see. They had a long piece of the paper by the time.
what was, what were some of the hymns they played here in the city though, about that time?

Oh, I can't think. A lot of them fellas got a lot of that music now, with Cornish had a whole lot of, close to Walt, or Dean, all those things. They didn't play that then, they didn't know it. Blue Red and all like that, they didn't know that. But it was hymns on that same order, you know. That was the only funeral they ever had a band with in the other example, when that boy died and we buried him.
But none of the other places had funerals, with music.
Yeah, yeah, they didn't have none in my home flat, none of the bad drugs, they didn't have none. Shreepo, oh yeah, that was the phone.

Oh yeah, you see, Shreveport, they never had no music for funerals around there at all, but they heard it by New Orleans. A lot of fellas coming down there and they'd see them funerals down there, you know, and some of them would remember. Well, they had a, he was a veteran from the Spanish-American War way back then. And it was his request to have some kind of music when you die, you know. So everybody knew I had been down this way, living down this way. They say, look, we got to have some kind of music at the funeral. I said, well, I'll tell you what you can do. I said, there ain't no brass band yet. We just make up the brass band and pay for them. What you charge for that? I said, oh, they used to charge about three or four dollars. I said, well, you'd have to pay about five dollars a piece. They said, no, I didn't want that many pieces, you know. I said, you don't know what the brass band is, do you? So they kept on saying, well, couldn't you kind of walk behind the hearse and play near Oh My God to thee or something like that, or some kind of church hand? Just use the cornet, just use. I said, you don't want no drum or nothing? I said, I can play any kind of way. They said, if you just want music. I said, yeah, I could play it. And say, when you get to the grave, play in the air, Oh My God to thee, say you use a veteran, say you go way out, buy the fence in the graveyard and make that last call there. I said, yeah, I can do that. I said, what'd that cost? I said, well, I mean, y'all, you ain't got no money. I said, I'll do it for ten dollars. So they paid me. Man, I come down to Texas Avenue, all the musicians, you know, they hang out around Jase's pool hall. They was all playing pool in there and they heard me blowing. What's that piece of, I said, near Oh My God to thee and they come out and seen the funeral. The fellas wanted me to wait, walk behind the hearse, you know what I said? I said, no, they don't do that the other way. Not in your honor. I said, let, they don't follow nobody to the graveyard. I said, let them follow you, you in front. Like the grand marshal said, you don't go behind the hearse that way. So I thought of that, you know, so I walked in front to her, leading the man to the grave. Brought him out there, you know, and got him out there. I played some kind of little hymn there. Then I went way out while he was bearing him in the corner of the yard, you know, way off. That's what it sounds sad though, you know, that I made that last call. And the fellow waved to me, you know, all over them. I'd make the call. And I'd come back to where they'd bury me back, you know, playing the air on my God as they'd let the preacher say a few words. And out we'd go. We didn't have to play going back, you know, just put my horn in the case. Had a little boy there tootin' my horn, I'd put you in the case. Went on up to the pool hall myself, you know. Then the fellow just laughed and said, man, what you doing in front of that hoist playing the air on my God to be? I said, man, how did he do that? Wouldn't you do it for ten bucks? And they all laughed then, you know. I said, come on, let's play some pool. I've got the pool again. I used to tell the fellas that I played a funeral by myself and they didn't believe me, you know. I said, go to Sweetport, they'll tell me. About when was that? That was way back. Let's see. That was about 1913. Just about. I might be missing it a year or two, but ain't many. 1913 or 14. That was about 20 bands playing. This one was playing, the next one playing. We was the last band, you know. We cut loose there with that piece that they played around. Oh, I can't think of it. We cut loose with that. They play what kind of pieces? They play at some special occasion or something? Or some neighborhood? No, Mardi Gras. They used to just all band, they call it the advertising band, you know. Chris Kelly, Rene A.
Buddy P.T., Sam Morgan, you know, they'd be bucking against one of them. One right behind them, one band on a big truck or something like that.

After Rene A. They play the next fella playing the next on down. So we was out of town dudes. We was hung on the last truck behind. Free music. That was in 1914. That was in 1914. I remember it coming to me. Mm-hm. We'd be bucking against one another, one right behind her and one band on a big truck or something like that. After Rene played the next fella playing the next on down. So we was out of town dudes, we was hung on the last truck behind. Free music. That was in 1914. I remember it coming to me.
What about the storm? Where were you when they had the big storm there?

Uh, 1915? Yeah, that storm. I was in Plagman, I believe. I was waiting for F.L. Trapani brother, jewelry store. I used to fix cloths. Fix cloths and fix bicycles. They turned the whole shop over to me, you know, the workshop. Used to sell instruments, recordings, guitars. You see, I knew how to tune them up. That's how I learned how to tune them up. Tune up, sell a fella a guitar and I'd tune it for him, you see. If he bought a violin, I'd sell him a violin, tune the violin up for him. Some fellas was just that dumb, they couldn't tune the instrument and they'd come back and still about a week after to get it tuned again. I'd tune it up for him again. But they found a way to get those little pipes, you know, fine, fine. You'd blow them that way and tune the instrument up. We used to sell them. I used to sell them. I used to sell that too. I waited for the plug in a long while.
Well you know something?
I wanted to ask you, which of those rags do you like that you play from the Red Bull now?
Well I tell you I like them all. I played with one of them. But the best thing I liked, Frog Legs, Easy Winner, Chrysanthemum, Ophelia Ryan. They're real musical numbers.
What numbers did they like down here in New Orleans in holding times?
They didn't play so many of them.
They didn't play them all, just some of them.

I catch one band maybe play one or two of them, and the other band maybe play two or three of them. I used to study them books. Cecilia kind of had books like that, but just for piano, you know. And boy she could play some piano. She learned that in England. And she finished college over there. She come over here and went to Boston Conservatory. Studied all over again and learned them books. And threw them in the wash shed, you know. In the wash house. They had a regular wash house. They had a bell from his house to mine and called me when they were going out. Maybe I'd have to go around and hitch the buggy up or something. When they'd be gone, I'd eat that wash shed. I'd get me a mattress down, put it on the floor and get one of them big books there. Me and that book all day looking at it, you know. I was trying to make out that music, but I couldn't read so well. And I'd spell like the devil. Man, I was making notes there and coming after whistling and singing. Then when I learned how to play cornet I used to try to play them, but you see it was piano music and I had to raise the guitar and it'd run too high. I couldn't make the notes. I'd come down and make it, you know. I got all confused. And when I got to Alexander they had those red books you see, but they couldn't get no cornet player to play them. I dived in there and me and Harry used to practice every day and say, eat your breakfast and come right on around to my house. And just like a man working, me and him would blow their antics, 12 o'clock and get dinner and come back, finish the evening. And man, we got something on it. Harry bought him on it. He climbed it and he had a B2 Albert system. So he changed that system. He was a great clarinet player. He got a baron system, A and B, and sold his old clarinet. Then we practiced showing up then because he had to learn that baron system, you see. Albert is different. And he used to play over in the District Cross to buy every night. You know, when you play every night that way you can track a lot of stuff. Playing them red books, you know.
A couple ways in line. A couple ways in line. A couple ways in line.
A couple ways in line. A couple ways in line. A couple ways in line.

A couple ways in line. It becomes so natural to you to do what? To play them books, I just play them by head. Whether I had them or not, I imagine I could see them. You all could see it. See the music. Just imagine I see it, you know, and play it. My pa said that was great before he died. I said a fella can imagine music like that and play it. It plays a great part in the musicianship. That's the fact. To play a piece the same way all the time you have to imagine you see the music in it. Because your argument wouldn't run that way. It would run a different kind of way altogether. Now if I had to fake a ride I'd just make anything that'd come in my head you see. But I just imagine I see that music. I was quick at that. Any piece to play, if I could play it and read it and play it, well if I didn't have the music I could play that piece. Don't care if it's new people. Just imagine I see it and play it. That's better than transparency.
I wanted you to tell us about that joining up with the young men, what that was like.

Well that was a society, you know. You pay so much, let me see, was it every week? Every quarter, they'd have a meeting just like the union. I don't know, I believe it was a dollar a quarter or something like that. I can't remember exactly, but anyhow, when you die they bury you, you see. They give you a funeral and your wife or who you may be made out to, your sister or something, she get so much money. But it wasn't very much a couple of hundred or something like that. But they bury you know. The time I got down there my wife had told the boys I was coming, you see. I had a job waiting for me in the Excelsior Band. And we was burying fellas every day, then two funerals a day. The fellas say, now why don't you get into the young men? That make the band more popular, you see. He said when you get in the band it'll always get your band to play for them, you know. And Peter was in one of them society too, Peter Burkhardt. I wanted to be right with the gang, you know, so I said I might as well get in one too. But sometime I'd get a funeral, you see. By being a member of that young man, you see. I'd get a funeral, give me the funeral, you know. So I'd ring up the boys, ring up the Excelsior Band. I said, I've got this one. Sometimes Willie Onfield would get a funeral uptown where he did that. See, he belonged to some of them societies too, you know. And his brothers too. All the musicians used to join for that purpose. Man, I joined that young man's society. I paid a dollar for that opportunity to join Gideon and that. So in the next quarter, they was voting, you know, for president one step or another. Them dudes right up there and start the fighting. I walked out. My wife said, what's the matter with them? I think a fellow named Willie Russell and the president, what they had at that time, they went together. Rear up to fight. One fellow had a pistol. I said, uh-uh. I said, I'll quit today. I just let them keep that dollar. I didn't want nothing to do with that society. I was there in it. I ain't never done nothing since but the union. We had a, what they call a union. We had a, not a union, they call it a pleasure club. We had a regular pleasure club. Didn't get nothing out of it. I stayed in there. I paid my dues and nothing until it was resolved. I drawed my money back. I got the money back off.
Well, what's the difference between a society and a pleasure club?

Well, you see, pleasure club, they just give something. Give a big dance, you know, and swell the treasure. They either, they'd have money for the half pastime sometimes, maybe they run a little excursion or something, on a boat or something like that. They used to do that. But the union is different, you see. The union is supposed to protect you with the music business that you play, you know.
Well who had the pleasure club? All the musicians or who?

Yeah, the musicians in town pretty much all of them was in there. And when they broke up, I got the money back. I got more than what I had spent in there. I got more money back. And Willie Hoffer took the charter I believe for him and said, give me the charter, I'll take that for my pay. Well he was lucky, he took it and used to, got up a union, you see. And he got that charter, bought that charter from Willie Hoffer I believe, $25. Chris Kelly was living there.
Which time? When they had the pleasure club or when they had the union?
When they had the union. He got in the union. I was in that union. That's the union. It turned out to be alright. That's the money we got done.
Well the pleasure club, who was heading out? You have a president?
Yeah I believe, let me see who was president. George Augustine. I think he was Dick.
What did he play?
Biggs.
Who else was in it that was the official or something?
Peteron, all them boys, Edith Pierce, and Siliccine.
They had officers?
Huh?
They had officers, they were leaders, all those guys.
Just for pleasure. That was the club. The club failed, you see, but the union didn't.
How many officers would a club have? They have a president?
President, secretary, treasurer, finance secretary. Then they have the board. Twelve members in the board.
Do they have any other benefits other than for death? Dariel?
They passed that in the meeting sometime. Our union, we get a deathier wife, get a thousand dollars. That's in town.
What about the young men of Algiers now sick? When you're sick, do you get a benefit there? Yeah.

I forgot how much you get, but they paid something for the doctor bill. All that kind of business. When you keep the bucket, it was a matter of getting two, three hundred dollars. After they buried, you see, they paid for the bill. They'd give us three or four hundred dollars, something like that.
But the pleasure club was also insurance too? Yeah.
Now the young men there, do they have a dinner or a banque or anything like that? Young men.

Yeah, the young men that you belong to? Yeah, they used to have a, once a year they'd have a little outing, you'd get two, three carriages of beer, big box, big box of ham sandwich, you know, like that, lemonade, punch. Oh yeah, big time they had signages, sometimes gumbo. Our union, we had one outing there, you was there wasn't you?
Yeah, I was there at the banque.
Yeah, me and Bill Russell had a whole ticket. Well that sounds about right.
Show boy was there too.
I didn't do any time when a hula hoop come out. Show boy had his hula hoop, twisting around there.
Well you were talking back when we first started talking about hoodoo and stuff, and you said do people, people used to believe in it more than they do today or you said people still believe in it?

Yeah, I got some people around there still believe in it. A fella asked me one day, I was going to the fella, said, he comes to the house, and he come out of Mississippi somewhere, I said, what is it? He said, do you know anything? I said, what you talking about? He said, I mean, do you, two-headed stuff. I said, two-headed stuff? What do you mean by two-headed? I ain't never seen nobody but one head. He said, yeah, but they tell me they got some people around you. You know, I was here and said they can tell you things like that. I said, anybody can tell you something. I don't believe in that stuff. I'll be frank with you. I said, just go around and ask something of them people around you, they'll tell you. I said, I don't believe in nothing like that. Every now and then somebody asked me that. Do you know anything or nobody could tell you something? Yeah, they say when I moved over here, they say they had some seven sisters or something. I don't know if they were close.
Seven sisters with the seven cats?

Seven sisters. They're no different things and all that. I come to find out some of these folks like Ron in the neighborhood. I don't know. I never did believe in nothing like that, but some people do. A lot of people believe in that.
Well, what do they do?

In a while back when I was a young kid, you used to believe in that all around on Rampart Street with the dealer all around up in there. You're going to keep a fool with me, I'm going to throw at you. Throw some hoodoo stuff. And every day I noticed, you know those little callers like? You know them long-billings of the guy and the people. You call them the rural. People come out early in the morning and get a lot and scrub their steps and have that number shining down like they're washing.
Why would they do that?
Scrub the steps off to keep the hoodoo in. They walk on up hoodoo and all that.
Well, they use brick dust I see for cleaning steps.
Yeah, brick dust, lawn, everything.
Will that brick dust keep hoodoo off?
Oh no, there ain't no such a thing as hoodoo.
Yeah, but I mean is that what it's supposed to do?
Yeah, that's what they think it'd do.
Well, what kind of stuff do they leave there?
I don't know what it could be. Special Indian slogan from way back, you know, the medicine man, what you call them? Hoodoo, witch doctor. And that's Indian, huh?
Yeah, that's Indian.

That comes from the Indian, you know, to a witch doctor. And they had another one you used to call the witch here. Used to have the picture of the old witch riding the broom. And black cat and all like that. That's why I named my piece like that. I got it in my name and the black cat on the fence. They say the old witch riding the broom. See on Halloween night, they have the paper cuttings, you know, the witch riding the broom, the black cat, round by a graveyard or something like that. Used to say that over the river. I believe I'll go to Al J and get me some graveyard. I know one thing I see a dude do in my hometown, Plagman. He comes from down there. He went and bought him a ton of red beans. And they bought a half a yard of red flannan, you see. And he put a bean in each piece of little flannan by the inch square. He took black thread and sewed it up like that. And he had a grip full of them beans in there. The whole time he come to Plagman and had a saloon there they called Doatree Saloon. You know, a fella used to gamble in the back, shoot craps and play card back, you know. That little table reminded me of this one. And it had a little chain all around it, you see. That was his alibi and he didn't receive no money, you see. He come in there and put that table there, attach that little chain up there like that. And got his grip and put it on the little bench right under the table, you know.
I said, what you going to do?

I said, man I'm going to sell some hand yesterday. I said, buy one of these and you'll never lose them. Put one of them beans on the table, you know. You couldn't see it wrapped up in that flannan, you know, and sewed with that black thread, you know, like a football. And they look real funny, you know. He took it out that grip, put one up there, you know. I said, you want to buy one? I said, just a dollar. The fella put a paper dollar down, took his bean, put it in his pocket, you know. I said, now what that do? See. That's luck. I said, boy, you can lose. You might lose a few dollars, but you'll win them back. Man, he went and told the other fellas about it. Just because he told them that, you see he went and tried it. He bet two, three dollars there and made a win. Told the other fellas, man, and that place got crowded. He had to shut the door. Everybody was buying the red beans. They sold up the planter. I had a little fella running around there looking at it, you know. I told my pa about it. Man, he sold out. Sold that grip of beans, you know, and went right on out and caught that 54 going up. Caught the train, went on to another state. See, got out of the state. Went all away from here and got rich. They had a suitcase of money done made off them dudes. Two, three fellas come in there and say, you know any other kind of luck charm you could fix for them? He said, yeah, boy. I said, I got some shoes. It's too bad. I'll sell you a pair of them shoes. He said, but you have to wait until next week, don't you? I have to, I got some shoes to order. He come down here on Ramport Street and get some of them cheap shoes, you know, about a dollar and a half a pair. Or two dollars or something like that. Bring them shoes up around that saw me the switches there. And like Platinum, Louisiana, Ford, Baton Rouge, you see. And he sell them shoes, $15. See, they're supposed to be fixed. You wear them shoes. Nobody can't do you nothing, you know. You ought to see them people buying them shoes, you know. My father looked at them and say, you know one thing, say they got some crazy people in the world.
You're right about that.

And he sold them shoes out. He'd take orders for about thirty-pack, you see. And he'd sell them shoes. People be there just like that to buy them shoes. Put them on. Then they'd go anyway, see. You wouldn't be scared. Nobody can't hurt me. I got on some shoes.
Well some of the guys in the band, you know, are pretty afraid. Yeah, they never did catch him.

You see, he wouldn't stay there long after he'd sell them shoes. He'd go and train and go on somewhere else, you see. He had an old conny little trick. Some of them fellas would be lucky too when he sell them beans to that. They was going to be lucky anyhow, you see. He'd hit a stream of luck and slash that bean down there. These fellas used to be terrible with that stuff around there. They ain't so bad, no.

John Casimir was scared to death of that stuff. Yeah? Oh yeah, you didn't know that? No, I didn't know that. Oh man, I saw Thomas Jefferson kid him one day at a parade. You know, make those motions like he was going to throw something on him. And Casimir was scared to death. He practically quit playing and it was his band.

We had a fella in Mississippi, we used to call him See Me Now. You know, why we give him that name? You know, comedian fellas is funny, you know. They see fellas do something funny and they make something out of it. This fella come up one day, they used to get passes, you see. Bring their sweetheart to the show or something like that. You get a pass, you could bring his gun, you see. Well, this was one of the canvas boys, you know. People was kind of scared of him too, said he was a fool. He always was fooling around in the grass with some kind of weed, you know. And he'd break a piece and put it in his pocketbook. And everybody on the show scared of him. So he come up to the boys one evening and say, I want a pass, I want two passes. I got some friends I want to bring them to the show tonight, see me now? And the boys looked at him, said you better get away from here, you crazy. He said, that's all I got to sell is tickets. I'm going to give you some tickets. He said, you know, I'll bring my girl out. Girl, see me now? So we laughed at him so much that we just call him, see me now, you see. We go on out with the show. So the boys got sick of this fella, you know. Some of them show people bleeding that stuff too, and the boys himself, come as to bleeding, see me now, was bad luck, you see. So we put Seaman off the show. What made him put them off? He was like silly, you know, crazy. He seen Earl Offred playing trombone, you know, and Earl used to play loud trombone, you know. And he was working putting up the tent, helping them fellas put up the tent. So he went to town and he just had a payday, you know, took his last money, some pawn shop, and got a trombone, bought himself a trombone. And he never had a lesson in his life. He couldn't play, you know. He come back down there, he seen the musicians getting all fine, you know. The boys come up and say, hey, them fellas looking for you, you better go help put up that tent. He said, from now on I ain't putting up no tent, I'm going to play trombone in the dance. The boys said, I know you crazy now. So he went up under the tent after the fellas put the tent up and was watching all around there. I pop up, I make no kind of noise, you know. When the band went out that day, he tried to follow the band. So dear to dear
See we're talking about Simi Now, you say he played trombone with the band even though

he never had a lesson. No, they didn't let him play. So they got the towel down, the boy seen him losing, thought he was going crazy. He told Simi Now, everybody was scared of him, they thought he was a hoodoo or something. So he told the policeman, that's a pretty good fellow, we don't want you to put him in there and keep him in there now. I said, but I want you to run one thing, he's following this show and you want to get rid of him. He said, you just arrest him and lock him up, tell this show get out of town. When he get out of town, you turn him loose. You turn him loose and let him go. He hasn't done anything, bothered anybody on the show. I think he's a good boy too, he said, but we don't want to carry him around like this. So the police done like he told him, took the boy and put him in jail on the show, got out of town. They turned him loose and he didn't know where the show was going. When we got in the next town, Simi Now was sitting on a bridge, you know, up on the railing, waving at the people. And they went to the show lot and putting up the tents, Simi Now was right there. And several times there wouldn't nobody tell him where we was going, you know, try to shake. And he would be in the town before the show get there. And how he get there, I don't know. But anyway, the boss put the police on him and told the police, he said, you keep him here three days and I know we won't see him no more. He said, turn him loose after three days. He was following the show and we don't want him with the show. Well, after he kept him three days and the show went on, we lost him. We didn't know where the show was at. But that's his state, you know, he must have known his state because every time they're leaving, he'd beat the show to the other town.
What state was that?
That was the Mississippi.
We're talking about the brass bands that played. Oh yeah. This guy Lazard you said had a band.

Joe Lazard, he was the leader of the Pacific band. And Buddy Johnson was in that band. Buddy Johnson. And Arthur Johnson wasn't in there because he was about nine, he was too young. And the baritone player was Joel Lazard, yeah. Joel Lazard? No, Joel Lazard was a cornet player. What kind of cornet?
B flat or E flat? B flat.
E flat. And I'm trying to get that baritone player. His name was... Well, we skipped him. Yeah, well, let's find out what Buddy Johnson played in that band. Buddy Johnson played trombone.
They have another trombone?
Sometimes Frankie Doosman would play. I think Gabriel played in that band too.
Gabriel?
Yeah. What instrument did he play? Clown there. He's dead. He used to be a plaster. Did he have a first name?
George Hooper.
What did he play? He played cornet at that time.
That was before he became a baritone player.
Yeah. George Simm, that's the baritone player. George Simm played baritone and George Hooper played cornet.
Were these Algiers fellas?
All the Algiers fellas right there. A fella named Davis. George Davis was the bass drummer.
Snag drummer? I'm trying to.
Dude, he got killed. Dude?
Did he play any other instrument?
No, he was just a drummer. And he played the drums in an orchestra, you know, different orchestras.
Who did he work with that you remember?
Used to wake up the man in the habit club with Frankie Doosman. I can't play with him. I knew dude the trumpet player.
You mean George Hooper? He died too. No, dude I can't play with. Oh no, he was a classer.
Brick man, you know. Yeah, you don't know his last name right there. Gabriel. Oh, dude Gabriel.
Dude, yeah, that was a man.

Yeah. Have any alto players or a mellophone peck on, you know? I see. Well, uh, at that time, uh, Jimmy Spriggs was the name, but they called him Jimmy Fall Out. Oh, you heard about him. He went out to the Creole Syncopy. He was a good band at that. He went out on the time, Pantages time. Around New York or around the time.
Did they make much of a hit, that Creole band?

I should say they did. That's the first band left there, you know. That went anywhere. Eddie Vincent, Big Eye Louie. Jimmy Fall Out. And Bro, I think Bro was the name. Not this young Bro that started out with us.
Wellman Bro, you mean then, huh? Yeah. Wait, with Duke Ellington, is that the same?
Yeah, that's the Bro.
Have a banjo player, a guitar player? Let's see, they used violin.

Yeah, the guitar player with them, but I don't know how kind of a drummer. Drama? Let's see. No, Freddie Kepard with them. Freddie Kepard, Big Eye Louie, Eddie Vincent, Jimmy Fall Out. Bro, he must have been some right there, a drummer.
I'm not sure, but I think maybe Dink Johnson played with them a while. Do you ever know him?
I heard about him, what he's a drummer is. Yeah. I guess Dink was with him there.
Phil Johnson's brother.

There's another Dink from Shreeport, you know, he's in Chicago now, Dink Stewart. What did he play? He's a tenor, D tenor sax player, and his brother was a man named Cliff. We had a band together, me and Dink Stewart, Dink, Shreeport.
Well, back to the Pacific band, what kind of jobs would they play?
Brass band, like the rest of these, but they mostly played parades at that time. Sunday, all day Sunday parades. Every Sunday some society turned out, you know.
Would they play mostly on this side or mostly on the other side?
They used to play on the other side, but mostly this side. All down that coast down down below the Navy.
McClendonville?

Yeah, used to walk on rocks, dirty roads. Way down far in Belichick. And on the Sunday they'd have a parade like Levy and go to Brittany and back. The next Sunday they'd go out in the night board somewhere.
What was the first brass band you ever played with when you came down here?
When I come down here? Yes sir. Alan.
Alan.

Who was in that band? Alan and a fella right in the M.O. Two Sweet, he was a carnage player. Alan and a man. And Yank Arthur Thomas, that's Buddy, Arthur Johnson, that's Buddy Johnson's brother. He was young like I was. Several other fellas. I used to play alto over there. Alan was playing cornet itself. I couldn't play enough cornet to play any bands, so they put me on the alto. Man I had one of them little upright alto that fell about that high, you know. Just making the chords, you know. And every time I'd get to the corner, you know, everybody looking at the cornet players, you know, patting their hands, you know. And I'd get along there and nobody wouldn't see me much, you know. I didn't like that much. I said I ain't no excitement at all. I said I know that I bet I'll make them look at me and get to the next corner, get to the next corner, you know. And I was supposed to play the cornet, you know, the chord, you know. I'd get to the chord and I'd say . And people just fall out and laugh, you know. Listen to that little fella say, he's rowdy, isn't he? I thought I was doing something. So Alan didn't like it much, you know. He said you don't have to make all that. He said just stay and make your C and your D in the chord that you're in. He said that's the alto. I wanted to make, I thought he was a great cornet player at that time. He couldn't play nothing. I thought he could though. Oh Alan had that little horn up in there, you know. And you missed one every time then, you know. You missed one, I tried to cover it up with the alto and everybody go to laugh, you know. I told him, go down there. I was like, you know, I'm sorry. So yeah, what broke me up. I went home and my poor had a little brass band around playing. Man, he's playing for Ray and one Sunday. Got everybody looking at the cornet players and trombone players and hollering, you know. And I got to the corner, went to make my little turn there, you know. I'm here to turn on the horn to the . Papa cut out from the front and come back there where I was and said, look, I'm telling you this. I don't have no music like that in my bag, you know. I'll send you back down that way you come from. I said, just make that one more time and you go home, you know. I said, all right, Papa. We went over the buy-in, Plankman, crossed the bridge, you know, all over that plane. Every time it would feel good to me, the music, I just had the bus I'd make when they'd run, you know, get around, a whole lot of people, you know. Man, they'd look around and say, look at little son, look at little son love. They used to call me son when I was little. Look at little son love, you know, man. They'd say that, that cuttle loop. Papa said, yeah, go on home. Give me that horn, yeah. Take my horn away from me. Send me on home. I'd go home crying, you know. Mama said, what's the matter son? I said, Papa put me out the bag. She'd go to the first. Yeah, I had to go when he said go, you know. I went home and cry all evening because they wouldn't let me put me in. Every time I'd get in the band, the Pa say, look, you going to bus out, show, I'd give you a job playing today, let you make a dollar and a half with me. He wouldn't pay me with other musicians, just give me a dollar and a half. I'd blow all day, you know. He said, I'm going to give you a dollar and a half now. He said, if you make a bus out, I'm going to send you right on home. Man, I just had to make that bus out. I'd watch him, you know, and get right in the middle place. Somebody would see me and I'd say, poop, poop, poop, poop, doodoo, doodoo. He'd look back, you know, and I'd go, doodoo, doodoo, doodoo. Trying to fool him, you know. He'd tell him, I heard you back there just now. I said, you know you can't fool me? He said, let's do that again now and right home you go. Well I wouldn't make that no more that evening. I'd be all right. So he kept the fool around until he found some other kind of instrument for me to play a tenor, upright tenor. I couldn't get them runs out on that, you know. He knew he heard me then. I'd play that tenor while. Make half notes, you know. Whole notes. I couldn't make my little run, you know. He'd show you on that one.
Did he play any fun with his band?

No, he didn't have no fun with Ron. He used to play for dancers mostly. And I tell you, he had to swell all because they used to sit down and make their own music. Just make up most of the whole program, the stuff they made up. And he used to have some dancers at that time. Quadrillion and lances. And he used to play shatters and zilting. And I said variety. And two steps, one steps. He used to play little rags too, and then he used to play sentimental music in the overtill. My father was a first class musician. You know what he could do? What's that? Just go to sleep at night like that sometimes, thinking about music and dream up, dream a piece. And he'd get up at two o'clock, every time in the morning, get his horn right away and play it. Keep from forgetting to play it and then he'd score it down, you know. Man, he'd get up the next day and play it. And my mother used to be his witness, you know, how that sounds kid? She said, that sounds lovely. She said, but it looked like it ought to have another part. Now see, you've got two parts, you ought to have three parts. That's a pretty novel. She said, I ought to be named, she'd give it a name too, you know. It ought to be named like something, some kind of flower or something like that. He'd get that down, he'd write it, write the lead of it, you know, and then he'd bring it around to Norrie Barber's house. And Norrie Barber was something like Seal, you know, he could score that stuff down, you know. He'd write the guitar part and the bandage, the guitar and the bass. Clarence William Paul was playing bass with him, Dennis William. He died up young building not so long ago. Just fix me to go see Clarence. He was working for the teepee railroad company.
Oh, tell about how old man Allen used to get jobs. Did you ever hear that story?

Yeah. Allen used to, yeah, you know, one of them societies, and the men would get some jobs, and the men would get sick, you know, it'd be low, you know. Allen would go see him, you know, go visit him. And if he just thought that man wasn't going to live like that, you know, he'd say, well, tell the family, the people, you know, if anything happened, just ring me up, let me know. See, I've got a band, you know, that'll see me. All right, Allen, you get the job. If anything happened to him, he'd come like one. Say, Frankie, yeah. And I got there and I'll leave open there. I think we're going to have one. I want you all to try them on, yeah. He said, all right, don't forget me now, yeah. He said, how is he? He ain't never know nothing about the man being singled. How is he? He put in the water, and he said, I don't know nothing about the man being singled. How is he? He put in the water, and he said, I don't think he'll last next week. He said, I want you, yeah. All right. Showing up about three or four days, the man died, you know. Frankie, you're about, you know, did you get that Allen? Yeah, yeah, everything's all right, bud. He said, oh, and get Carnish, you know. Carnish used to do that too. Tell me your man sick if he belongs to some kind of society. Carnish go see him, you know, how is he sick? He come in, you know, and he said, have a seat. How is he sick? He said, well, he ain't doing so good. He said, he's pretty weak. He said, yeah, I see. Look like, do he eat much? He said, yeah, he eats a little bit. Yeah, I said, poor fellow, I know him a long time. He said, look like he ain't going to make it. He said, yeah, he's pretty weak. Carnish go down the street. See, Louisa Armstrong, he said, what you doing next week? He said, well, I ain't got nothing next week. I'm going to hire you. I got a funeral in a couple of days.
Hire the man before the man die, you know.

They be pretty low. He know he's going to die, you know. He just say, you just watch out past you every day. I'll let you know. Next day you go see that man again, you know. You see him getting weaker than he can go to hire everybody he could get.
They used to do that around there.

That's where I used to get little jobs, you know. They had me doing that kind of thing. I said, I'll be about to go on back to Platt when there ain't much to do in that. Man dying, you got the way to do dying to get the job.
Well, did you all ever play for a woman or anything?

No, they had one woman I believe, yeah, sometime ago, 19… I don't know, I can't think of the date. My wife might think of it, but we ain't been so very long. She's a big woman, belongs to an old gang in society. And they hired a band for her. That's the only one I could remember, an old man, you know.
Well why don't they play for women?
It seemed like they ought to care for mother moving down there. And they got a lot of lady societies. The hoops, that whole thing, that's a lady society. But they don't bury them.
Well, lots of times the women march when the men are buried, I mean.

Yeah, ladies and all like that. They march with the band. Now that's the secret order, the Masons. Like the Masons, they got the ladies, turns out, too, you know, they wear cream suits. And they have, some of them have the drilling uniform, right? They have the sword. And they carry their little march on that, you know. The hardfellas, they got ladies, too. The hardfellas in the Elves.
What about the Pickwick band?
What ever happened to them? Did they have a Pickwick band here?
Oh, that was a long time before my time. My father was a young man then. He used to come down here. I'll tell you some fellas was playing in that band. The country.
Which one?

The old man. The old man. They come from Mombardo first there somewhere. Yeah. Well, Deconjay and, let me see who else was in that band. Deconjay. I believe old man Dominguez, the bass player, was in that band. Paul Dominguez daddy. He's a bass violin and a bass player, too. He was one of the best bands in the city. DeRooks was in that, too. Old man DeRooks. The boy's father. Old man DeRooks. He was a great company player. I don't know the boys. What are their names? I don't know them boys. They play music? They play music? Dolly got a bunch of little nephews. They play music now? Dolly got a bunch of little nephews. Oh. Yeah. They play modern jazz. Yeah. They play swell. I don't know the boys. What are their names? I don't know them boys.
They play music?
Lawrence and what is it?
They play music now?
Oh yeah, Dolly got a bunch of little nephews.
They play modern jazz?

Yeah, they play as well. Dolly plays piano, you know, she's swell piano. And she play bass violin too. Lawrence play piano, she play the bass. Lawrence is the cornet player and the trombone player. Donnie lived right around the block. Right around. That's what worried in that little woman about there, about to get away from me. He was a nice trombone player. He worked with me when I was in the WPA band. He split the band in two. He wouldn't let me in that band. You know when they first got up, they had about two hundred members. They had about fifteen band players. Used to come to Petone's place in the fifth world, athletic club. I was working there, me and Walter, DeCruz, the piano and the other big hard drum. You talk about a band, you ought to hear that band. Trombie, piano and drum. Play more music in six pieces. And we played everything. Joe's a theme. You know those pieces they call them, My Joe's a theme? The real, we had music for that. People used to come sit down and listen to that band and say I don't see how they can do that. One fellow come in one night and invite the band to come and have a drink with them to the bar. Me and Ellick went in there and Walter was on one side, me and Ellick on this side, you know. He'd say, call the rest of the fellas in. Come on. Give us all the cocktails. He'd say, why the rest of the band? He'd say, this is it, this is it. He'd say, me, you mean to say you three fellas play all that music I heard in that? He'd say that's the only band he got there. He'd say I got to see that. He'd come in there and sit down right by the bandstand. He had a little bandstand there about wide at that door there. Just big enough for me to sit on and the piano, you know, sitting this way. And me right by Walter and Ellick were right down on the floor. And people used to pass down there and that music, they'd come in there. It's the way Walter played that piano, you know. He had a heavy bass and a compliment. And when I lead he'd just make chords, you see. And I'd play about two chords and cut out. Then he'd play the piece on the piano, you know. The piano is a band by itself. When he'd go to playing like that, well instead of me setting up there and holding my lap, I'd grab my derby, you see, place the horn in the derby and make an off melody like what he was playing. And that made it sound like an alto sax, you see. And some chords he made that sound like a tenor or something like that. And you'd swear they had strings and everything in that band. And Ellick was a light drummer, you know. People would be dancing out in the street and they'd come inside, you know, and say, them three fellas there making that music, they'd say, yeah, I don't believe it. And they'd sit down to look after a while, the place would be full, people would come in and see who was playing. And they used to say, I don't see how they can do that. We couldn't see either, but we used to do it. After a while, there come Peter on some of them, they'd sit down and enjoy the stuff, listen out to us playing. And all at once Walter went crazy about this watchtower business. He had books, a gang of books on his arm going around selling them and a draft for him. He turned out to be a preacher one time. He forgot his music. He couldn't play an outfit to save your life, not like that. He wanted to play like Steve Lewis and a whole lot of other fellas, you know. And he couldn't do it. It wasn't in him to play that way. He had a nice style of playing. The only fella was doing that in the city. I used to love to play with him. He played soft and loud. Always had a job. When he got to studying that Jehovah's Witness, he'd come as to drinking whiskey. He drank so much that he started me off drinking. I used to see him enjoying himself so much, you know, until he'd get too bad and then I'd cut out. When he got to studying them books, why I didn't go with me, I pulled out from him. This fella used to be with him, Joe Rennie, you know the one. He's a bishop, man. Yeah, he's a big man.
Yeah, he's a bishop now. He wears a big black gun.
He's the one learning water, all that stuff. I jumped off the bus up on Jackson and dried one night and jumped right in his arms. He said, Lord, look at y'all. That's my hot friend, Charlie Love.
That's something that reminded me of something else I wanted to ask you. What different religions did you used to play for? Religion?
Yeah. At funerals?
Yeah. Like Baptists and… Catholic. You all did play music for Catholic funerals? In flag one, that's all they were.
Catholic. No, I mean music for funerals.
Oh, funerals.
What religions would hire a band?
Oh, Baptist people, art fella. Catholics, they don't have music.

They never did? Well, once in a while like that, some fella belonged to the Catholic Church. If he desires music and asked for it, say he want music when he dies, when he dies, the Catholic Church, if you desire music and ask for it, you know, say you want music when you die, the band will come bring your body to church but they don't play. They just march behind, you know, the grand marshal and they bring the body into church and the band waits for you. And when they come out of church they don't play. When they get in the next block of Wesleyan Church then they start playing. Then I'd like the Methodists they'll have, and the Baptists, and the Elves and different societies like that, but the Catholics don't
have anything. Well I knew they didn't anymore, I just wondered

if they used to. No they never did. If a fellow desires isn't going with the Catholic, then they can bring them to the Catholic Church, but they don't have that music. They walk, when they get in that block they don't play, they walk to the church and they bring the band, this band, and wait for them until the family goes. They get back in line and they get in the next block they play. But they won't do like that church. There's nothing in the Catholic religion, in the Bible, you see. Most Catholics are the Father of Christ, Jesus Christ, and he didn't have no music. And he could do that and you. Now, the Jewish people, it's funny, I remember in Shreepo we played for a Jew win. We had our uniform and everything on, you know, went into it. We was up in the balcony, went up there and I went up there and pulled my hat off, you know. Went in up there and the fellow come there, took my hat and said, put your hat on in there. I said no, I'm going to put my hat on there and pull it off. You know, you go out in there and pull it off. When you go out of the door, when you go outside, you take it off. That's funny, isn't it? Differently, you know, I felt. I said nothing down, you know, and took my hat off, you know, had it on my lap. The fellow come from way downstairs up there, seen that, you know. And then he went up there and said, put my hat on. And he said, put my hat on. I said, no. Can't do that. You're going to do it if you stay in there. You slapped it on. Pull it off when you go outside. So when you go outside take that off. Don't wear it off. And another thing I see them do after they marry, they got something in two glasses that they gave them, the fellow gave them his wife. She drank and he took one and he drank like that. And they break that glass. Throw it down. Bam! Break that glass all over. I never did find out what that was. It's wine. Huh? It's wine. But they break the glass. That's a meaning to that.
Say, you said there was no Excelsior at one time? No Excelsior brass band?

Not when they had the Pequik band there was no Excelsior. But after the Excelsior went out of existence, then they had, after the Pequik went out of existence, then they had the Excelsior band. That was just as good, you know, almost. Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm . Mm-hmm .

segments.title: Opening of the 1960 interview and a hoodoo song
segments.summary: Allen identifies the location (Love's home in Algiers) and the date; Love sings the chorus of a hoodoo song he sang at 16 or 17 and gives his birth date, October 6, 1885.

segments.title: Hoodoo songs and the Marie Laveau song
segments.summary: Love says many people still believe in hoodoo and that old songs were written about it, including a Marie Laveau song Papa Celestin used to sing.

segments.title: Singing 'I've Been Hoodooed' in the Overton minstrel show
segments.summary: Love recalls the song in old minstrel shows, with Billy Kersands doing the vest-stripping act on the Overton and Senior Ragtime Minstrel Show trip through Mississippi around 1916.

segments.title: Billy Kersands and his wife Louisa
segments.summary: Love describes Kersands' wife Louisa, who taught him his act and covered for him when he forgot his lines.

segments.title: Kersands' jokes, the English queen, and the impostor John Johnston
segments.summary: Love recalls Kersands' chicken joke, how he made a solemn queen laugh in England, his spending and drinking, and a big man in the show who was mistaken for him in Mississippi.

segments.title: What 'coon' means in the song
segments.summary: Allen asks the meaning of the word in the song and Love says it means a big black man.

segments.title: First coming to New Orleans as a child
segments.summary: Love says he partly lived in New Orleans as a baby and boy, staying with his cousin Henrietta from about age ten until sixteen.

segments.title: Streetcar screens and the growth of segregation
segments.summary: Love says streetcars were mixed when he was a boy, and that the screens went up around 1950, including in Shreveport despite a local fight against them.

segments.title: Rough districts: Franklin Street, Rampart and the Battlefield
segments.summary: Love and Allen work out where the tough, loud, fast neighborhoods were around Franklin, Rampart and Claiborne.

segments.title: Chinatown on Common Street and opium
segments.summary: Love describes the old Chinatown near Rampart and Common, tong killings, and opium smoking.

segments.title: Musicians who smoked hop: Moe Shelson's pipe
segments.summary: Love tells how his Shreveport band stole violinist Moe Shelson's clarinet-like opium pipe as a prank and how smoking darkened him.

segments.title: Bands that played the Red Book and Bunk Johnson's uncle Willie Young
segments.summary: Love lists the Alexandria bands that played the Red Book and rehearsed together on Sundays, and describes Willie Young, Bunk Johnson's uncle, as a faker.

segments.title: Working the Alexandria district and its houses
segments.summary: Love recalls the district's 18 bands, the musicians who worked in them, and the madams he worked for.

segments.title: High water in Alexandria
segments.summary: Love describes a flood when the Red River rose into the district and he left until the water went down.

segments.title: Organizing a 50-piece funeral band for a dead Alexandria musician
segments.summary: Love tells how Alexandria musicians pooled money for a funeral for a musician killed by a train, and how he conducted the 50-piece band in 1908.

segments.title: Hymns and funeral music in New Orleans and elsewhere
segments.summary: Allen and Zander ask what was played at funerals; Love says only a few hymns like Nearer My God to Thee were known then.

segments.title: Playing a Shreveport veteran's funeral alone for ten dollars
segments.summary: Love tells how he led a solo cornet funeral procession in Shreveport for a Spanish-American War veteran and joked with the pool-hall musicians afterward.

segments.title: Mardi Gras advertising bands on trucks
segments.summary: Love recalls the competing advertising bands on trucks at Mardi Gras, with his out-of-town band last on the truck in 1914.

segments.title: The 1915 storm and working in the Trapani jewelry shop
segments.summary: Love says he was in Plaquemine at the time of the storm, working in a jewelry store workshop where he repaired clocks and bicycles and tuned instruments for sale.

segments.title: Favorite rags from the Red Book and what New Orleans bands played
segments.summary: Love names the Red Book rags he likes best and says New Orleans bands each played only a few of them.

segments.title: Teaching himself from piano books and practicing with Harry
segments.summary: Love tells how he studied Cecilia's piano books in a wash shed as a boy and later practiced the Red Book every day with clarinetist Harry in Alexandria.

segments.title: Playing music by imagining the page
segments.summary: Love explains how he plays pieces from memory by picturing the music, and why that matters in musicianship.

segments.title: Joining the Young Men's benevolent society
segments.summary: Love explains how burial societies worked, why musicians joined them to get funeral jobs for the Excelsior Band, and how he quit after a fight over an election.

segments.title: The pleasure club and how it became the union
segments.summary: Love explains the difference between a pleasure club and a union, who ran the club, and how the charter was bought to form the union.

segments.title: Union and society benefits, officers and outings
segments.summary: Love and Allen discuss officers, death benefits, sick pay and the annual outings of the union and the Young Men.

segments.title: Whether hoodoo is real; scrubbing steps with brick dust
segments.summary: Love says he does not believe in hoodoo but describes people asking him about it and the Rampart Street practice of scrubbing steps.

segments.title: The red beans and lucky shoes con man; musicians afraid of hoodoo
segments.summary: Love tells of a man who sold flannel-wrapped red beans and 'fixed' shoes as luck charms in Plaquemine, and Allen adds that John Casimir was scared of hoodoo.

segments.title: See Me Now, the crazy trombonist who followed the show
segments.summary: Love tells about a canvas man on a Mississippi tent show nicknamed See Me Now who bought a trombone and kept beating the show to the next town.

segments.title: The Pacific Brass Band and its Algiers members
segments.summary: Love names the Pacific band's leader Joe Lazard and its cornet, trombone, baritone and drum players from Algiers.

segments.title: The Creole Band and Jimmy Fall Out
segments.summary: Love talks about the Creole Band, the first New Orleans band to travel, and its members including Freddie Keppard, Big Eye Louie and Jimmy Fall Out.

segments.title: What the Pacific band played and where
segments.summary: Love says the Pacific band mostly played Sunday society parades on the Algiers side and down the coast.

segments.title: Love's first brass band: playing alto and getting sent home by his father
segments.summary: Love tells how as a boy he played alto in Alan's band, showed off at street corners, and his father sent him home for it.

segments.title: His father's dance band and how he composed
segments.summary: Love says his father's band played dances and lancers and rags, and describes how he dreamed up pieces and had them scored.

segments.title: Getting funeral jobs by visiting sick society members
segments.summary: Love and Allen describe bandleaders such as Allen and Carnish who visited dying society members to line up the funeral job in advance.

segments.chapter: Funeral customs, Pickwick band and later years
segments.title: Funerals for women and ladies' societies
segments.summary: Zander asks whether bands played for women; Love says it was rare, and describes lady societies marching with the bands.

segments.chapter: Funeral customs, Pickwick band and later years
segments.title: The Pickwick band and the Douroux family
segments.summary: Love recalls musicians in the old Pickwick band, including Dominguez and old man DeRooks, and the nephews of Dolly who play modern jazz.

segments.chapter: Funeral customs, Pickwick band and later years
segments.title: Trio at Petone's with pianist Walter and Walter's turn to religion
segments.summary: Love describes his three-piece band with a pianist and a drummer that sounded like a full band, and how the pianist turned to Jehovah's Witness books and drinking.

segments.chapter: Funeral customs, Pickwick band and later years
segments.title: Which churches hired bands: Catholic, Protestant and Jewish funerals
segments.summary: Love explains that Catholic funerals bring the body to church without music and that Protestant groups hire bands, and recalls a Jewish wedding in Shreveport.

segments.chapter: Funeral customs, Pickwick band and later years
segments.title: The Excelsior and Pickwick brass bands
segments.summary: Allen asks about the Excelsior band, and Love says it came after the Pickwick band went out of existence.
